source.title: Neural Spectral Capacity with Residual Context for Heterogeneous Resource Allocation within Transformers
source.authors: Chen-Yu Zhu; Ruo-Yu Zhao; Zhi-Chao Lu

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares trained performance for different architectures at comparable parameter budgets, including paired reversals with the same projection shapes and NSC score. This bears on V4 and shows that architecture placement can affect performance more than a claim of only slight effects would suggest.
record.gate_note: The paper cites empirical scaling laws but does not fit or test power laws in parameters, tokens, or compute, nor a compute-optimal allocation trend. It also reports downstream accuracies and architecture-ranking correlations, but those do not test predictability from scale or pretraining loss. Rows below cover reported loss and perplexity results for trained architectures.
record.test_reason: The study trains six width allocations from scratch at near-matched parameter counts (121M and 374M) and reports held-out FineWeb-Edu loss (Table 10). This bears on V4 in a new setting: heterogeneous per-layer residual and FFN widths, and layer order, at fixed depth. It fits no scaling laws, so V1–V3 and V5–V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that ResNSC gives higher eight-task accuracy than NSC at every matched LoNAS-LLaMA-7B pruning budget (+3.28 to +5.46 points), and that reversals hurt under weight inheritance too. They frame the matched-parameter differences as consequential, not as a test of shape-insensitivity.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not fit loss scaling laws. It trains selected Transformer architectures at two sizes and compares their held-out losses under different width allocations and orderings.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary with width-allocation method and ordering, pretraining scale, dataset, and scoring ablation.

fits_no_version.finding: In LoNAS-LLaMA-7B pruning with inherited weights, reversing FFN-width placement at the same parameter count lowers Avg8 accuracy from 68.87% to 59.49%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: At a fixed parameter count, placement of layer widths in pruned, weight-inherited models strongly affects downstream accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: At matched parameters, LAMBADA perplexity varies by 20–25% across allocations even though held-out pretraining loss varies by only about 2%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small shape-induced differences in pretraining loss can correspond to large differences on specific downstream perplexities.

record.problems: The 374M results and 121M ablations use one full run plus two final-decay continuations; their reported standard deviations measure annealing variation rather than independent full training runs. The 121M main comparisons use three independent runs.
record.rows_left_out: Downstream accuracies, WikiText/LAMBADA results for the main Table 2 architectures, and architecture-ranking correlations were left out because they do not directly measure the V4 loss claim or add distinct evidence beyond the held-out loss rows. Table 5 ranking correlations and the LoNAS pruning accuracy results are not scaling-law tests.

untested.parts: Depth is fixed per scale (16 and 24 blocks), so depth-versus-width aspect ratio is not varied. Only two scales are covered. Head count and other architecture details are held fixed.
No scaling sweep or power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
No compute-optimal search; the token budget simply follows a Chinchilla-style 20 tokens per parameter.
No power-law tests outside text pretraining. The AutoFormer ranking results concern score–accuracy correlations.
No test of whether downstream accuracy is predictable from scale or loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'challenges' label for the reversals is not warranted for V4. Matched-parameter held-out loss differences, including the reversals, stay within about 1.5–2.4%, consistent with Kaplan's few-percent shape effect. The differences are systematic and well beyond run or annealing noise, and the authors treat them as meaningful. The 374M runs and the 121M ablations use one run plus two final-decay continuations, so their error bars understate seed variance. The study's own method being better than baselines is not itself evidence on V4; only the size of the spread matters.

versions.untested_parts: No scaling sweep or power-law fit in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of substantially larger runs.
No search for loss-minimising parameter and token counts across compute budgets.

Tests selected width allocations and paired reversals at two pretraining scales; it does not isolate the causal effect of depth versus width or systematically vary each architectural feature independently.
AutoFormer architecture-ranking results are not tests of power-law scaling in image models or other modalities or training regimes.
Reports downstream accuracies, but does not test whether they improve predictably with scale or pretraining loss.
Does not compare scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal splits under different fitting choices.

relationships.reason: Loss spread across all allocations, including the reversals, is about 0.05 nats (1.7%) at 121M and 0.06 nats (2.4%) at 374M. Scoring-ablation architectures differ by up to 4% in FineWeb perplexity (about 1.4% in loss). Rows r1–r22.
relationships.display_finding: Loss spreads were about 0.05 nats at 121M parameters and 0.06 nats at 374M, or 1.7% and 2.4%, while scoring-ablation architectures differed by up to 4% in perplexity, about 1.4% in loss.

labels.condition: Six heterogeneous width allocations and orderings at near-matched parameters, 121M (16 blocks) and 374M (24 blocks), FineWeb-Edu held-out loss
labels.reason: Table 10 gives loss ranges of 2.96496–3.01478 at 121M and 2.61025–2.67282 at 374M, approximately 1.7% and 2.4%. Table 3's FineWeb perplexity spread corresponds to approximately 1.4% in loss. These small differences support V4 within the tested setting, despite consequential ordering effects.

relation.reason: Its own near-matched-parameter architecture comparisons measure held-out pretraining loss and therefore test V4.

tranche.reason: Heterogeneous per-layer widths and paired reorderings provide a new setting bearing on V4. The tested pretraining-loss differences remain small; the study fits no scaling laws.

source_check.notes: The 374M results and 121M ablations measure annealing variation, not independent full-training variability. Support is confined to selected width allocations at fixed depths; instruction/chat and reasoning training are not tested.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Uniform, VWT, TLM, NSC and ResNSC allocations at 121M and 374M, excluding the paired reversals
reader_labels.reason: Held-out loss differences across these allocation choices are modest in the reported runs; rows r1–r5 and r7–r11.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.reason: Reversing the same projection-shape inventory worsens held-out loss at both scales, showing that placement can materially affect performance; rows r6 and r12.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The tested scoring variants do not have a uniform effect across datasets; depth-only and no-propagation variants achieve lower LAMBADA perplexity than full ResNSC; rows r25 and r27.
